sections.title: Language models follow instructions
paragraphs: Unlike smaller {{model}}s that memorize patterns from labeled pairs, {{largeLanguageModel}}s have learned so much text that they respond to instructions written in plain language. You condition behavior by describing what you want — no training examples required.
The {{prompt}} is your interface. Write clear task wording, provide context if needed, and the {{model}} generates a response shaped by what you asked. Change the prompt and the answer changes too.
This is why prompting is central to LLM work. You do not retrain {{weights}} for every task; you rewrite instructions to steer what the {{model}} already knows.

In AiEval you will compare {{model}} answers to the same prompt. That comparison only works when the prompt is clear enough that different models understand the goal — another reason prompt quality matters from day one.
Next: comparing answers. Once you can write a clear prompt, the question becomes: which {{model}} followed it best?
bullets: {{prompt}} — the instruction text you send to the {{model}}.
{{largeLanguageModel}} — a {{model}} trained on enough text to follow new instructions.
Condition, don't retrain: rewrite the prompt, not the {{weights}}.

check.prompt: A colleague wants to classify support tickets as urgent or not. They suggest: "Let's fine-tune a {{model}} for every new ticket category." What is the faster first step?
check.answer: Write a clear prompt describing urgent vs not-urgent, then test on real tickets
choices: Collect 100,000 labeled tickets and train a small classifier from scratch
Write a clear prompt describing urgent vs not-urgent, then test on real tickets
Run automation on blank prompts and hope the model infers the task
Ask every customer to label their own ticket before submitting
check.explanation: {{largeLanguageModel}}s can classify from a good {{prompt}} alone — no fine-tuning needed. Test prompt wording first; train only if prompting proves insufficient.

sections.title: Clear wording, clear results
paragraphs: Ambiguous prompts produce varied answers. If you write "Summarize this document," one {{model}} might give three bullets while another gives ten sentences. Neither is wrong because "summarize" did not specify length or format.
Good prompts constrain the task: what inputs to expect, what output format, what tone, and what to avoid. The more specific your instruction, the less room for misinterpretation.
Click each example below to see how wording shifts the answer. Notice that vague prompts allow creativity the task may not want.
When building evaluations you will later judge which answer is better. That judgment is easier when the prompt leaves no question about what "better" means.

reveals.reveal: The {{model}} guesses length, style, and focus — different runs may give very different outputs.

reveals.prompt: Prompt: "Summarize in three bullets for a technical audience." → What happens?
reveals.reveal: The {{model}} knows: three items, bullet format, skip lay explanations. Output is predictable.
The {{model}} invents a scale (1–5? A–F?), guesses criteria, and may not explain reasoning.

reveals.prompt: Prompt: "Score this essay 1–5 on clarity, using the rubric below." → What happens?
reveals.reveal: The {{model}} uses your scale, your criterion, and can reference the rubric for consistency.

check.prompt: You want a {{model}} to extract customer names from support emails. Which prompt is clearest?
check.answer: Extract the customer's full name from the email. Return only the name, no explanation.
choices: Extract the customer's full name from the email. Return only the name, no explanation.
check.explanation: The third option specifies what to extract (full name), what input (email), and what output format (name only). The other prompts are too vague for reliable automation.

sections.title: From prompt to evaluation
paragraphs: Once you can write a good prompt, the next question is: which {{model}} or which version answers best? That is where evaluation enters.

In AiEval you will send the same prompt to multiple {{model}}s, collect their answers, and compare quality using a {{rubric}}. The prompt must be clear enough that all {{model}}s understand the task — otherwise you are comparing apples to oranges.

Later lessons cover how to break "better" into scorable {{criterion}} rows. For now, remember: prompting is not just asking questions; it is defining the task clearly enough to judge the answers fairly.
Next up: comparing answers — same prompt, different models, measurable quality.
bullets: Good prompts enable fair comparison across {{model}}s.
Vague prompts lead to varied answers that are hard to score.
Evaluation depends on clear task definition — your prompt is that definition.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is a {{prompt}} in the context of a {{largeLanguageModel}}?
check.answer: The instruction text sent to the model
accept: the text that tells the model what to do
check.explanation: The {{prompt}} is the instruction you send. It conditions what the {{model}} generates without retraining {{weights}}.
